prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Do not use colons.

text:
On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted from Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing, and by then the public had grown a little bored with such trips. Commander Jim Lovell was a veteran on his fourth flight into space. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was making his first. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and grounded, and Swigert stepped in with almost no warning.

The first two days went smoothly. The crew named their command ship Odyssey and their lunar lander Aquarius, and they settled into the routine of a long coast through space. On the evening of April 13, they were about 200,000 miles from home and roughly fifty-six hours into the flight. They had just finished a television broadcast that few networks bothered to carry. Mission Control then asked them to do a routine chore, which was to stir the supercritical oxygen and hydrogen stored in tanks aboard the service module. Stirring kept the contents from stratifying and kept the gauges accurate.

Swigert flipped the switch. Moments later a bang shook the spacecraft. Swigert reported, "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it, changing the wording slightly, and the understatement entered history.

What the crew did not yet know was that oxygen tank number two had ruptured. Years earlier, during ground testing, the tank had been damaged and its wiring insulation weakened. When the stirring fans ran, a spark jumped across the exposed wires and ignited the insulation inside a vessel full of pure oxygen. The blast tore off a panel on the side of the service module and crippled the neighboring tank. Oxygen began leaking out into space. Without oxygen, the fuel cells that made electricity and drinking water for the command ship would soon die.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and his teams watched the readings fall. Lovell, looking out a window, saw a stream of gas venting into the void and understood that the problem was no mere instrument fault. Within about three hours Odyssey was nearly dead, its battery power reserved for the final descent to Earth. The only option was to turn the lunar module into a lifeboat. Aquarius had been built to support two men for two days on the Moon's surface. Now it would have to keep three men alive for four days.

The next question was how to get home. Mission planners had put the spacecraft on a path that would not return to Earth on its own. Abandoning the idea of landing, they considered turning around immediately, but the service engine might not be safe to fire. Instead they chose to swing around the Moon and use its gravity to sling the ship back. About five hours after the explosion, the crew fired the descent engine of Aquarius, a stage never designed to push a docked spacecraft, to place them on a path that would return to Earth. They passed behind the Moon, higher above its far side than any humans before or since, and then fired the engine again to speed the trip home.

The long journey back brought new troubles. Aquarius carried power for only a short stay, so the crew shut down nearly everything to conserve electricity and water. The cabin grew bitterly cold, dropping to near freezing, and condensation beaded on the walls. The men slept little. Haise developed a painful fever from a urinary infection, and everyone drank far less than the body needs.

The most dangerous problem was the air. Carbon dioxide from the astronauts' breathing was building up in the cramped lander, and the filters that removed it were running out. The command module held plenty of spare canisters, but they were square, while the sockets in the lunar module were round. People on the ground gathered the same sorts of items the crew had aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a suit hose, and a roll of duct tape. They worked out a clumsy adapter and read the steps to the crew over the radio. The men built it as instructed, and the carbon dioxide readings dropped. It remains among the best-known improvisations in the history of spaceflight.

Meanwhile, engineers faced another puzzle. Odyssey had never been meant to be switched on again after being shut down in flight, and the procedure for restarting it had to be written from scratch. Ken Mattingly, the astronaut who had been grounded, worked in a simulator for long hours, testing sequences that would wake the ship using as little power as possible. The result was a checklist that the crew could follow after days of cold and fatigue.

As they approached Earth, the crew separated the damaged service module. Looking at it for the first time, they saw that an entire side panel was missing and that the wreckage trailed debris. The sight confirmed how close they had come to disaster. Then they let go of Aquarius, which had saved them, and prepared for reentry in the command module alone.

Reentry brought one last tense wait. Every returning Apollo crew passed through a few minutes of radio silence while a sheath of hot plasma surrounded the capsule. For Apollo 13 the blackout seemed to stretch on, past the expected time, and the people in Mission Control listened to static. After a long pause Swigert's voice came through. Parachutes bloomed over the South Pacific, and on April 17 the capsule splashed down close to the recovery ship, the USS Iwo Jima, after a flight of nearly six days.

The three men were thin, dehydrated, and exhausted, but they were alive. Lovell never did walk on the Moon. His fourth flight would be his last.

An investigation board traced the accident to the tank design and the testing that had damaged it. NASA redesigned the tanks, removed the stirring fans' electrical hazards, and added a spare battery and extra oxygen to the service module. The program flew four more lunar missions before it ended.

Today the story is remembered less as a failure than as a model of teamwork under pressure. Aquarius had never been intended as a lifeboat, and no checklist covered what happened. The crew and thousands of people on the ground solved each problem as it arrived, with whatever was at hand. Apollo 13 was a mission that failed to reach its goal and succeeded at something more important, which was bringing everyone home.
